Interviewer:	OK, we are interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines – people in their 2nd year.  We’re mainly interviewing people that are going on placement, because we want to know why they’re going on placement and what they expect to find out and we’re going back to them, when they’re on placement, again – but you’re not going on placement?

Subject:	No, I was on the placement programme but then I changed to the actual one without the industrial placement.

Interviewer:	Well I’d be quite interested in why you made that decision then, that’s why we wanted to talk to you as well. The things that we’re looking at are why women decided to do engineering and hopefully try to improve women’s retention in the industry. At the end of the 2 year project, we’re going to put together a big guidance document (yes) and give it back to the Engineering Council to hopefully improve the situation for women (right) in engineering. So I’ll start off just asking you a few background questions about why you decided to do engineering and that.  Is it aeronautical engineering that you’re doing?

Subject:	Yeah, aeronautical, yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you doing the masters course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK. What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did French, Maths, Further Maths and Physics.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Comprehensive – normal high school.

Interviewer:	It wasn’t an all girls’ school or anything?

Subject:	No, just a regular.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous experience in the industry?

Subject:	Before I decided to do engineering at uni?

Interviewer:	Or while you’ve been at uni?

Subject:	Erm, no I wouldn’t say – I mean I worked at [company] but that’s more agricultural engineering and I worked in their marketing department, so didn’t have any hands-on experience or anything because it was business really.

Interviewer:	What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	Erm, no, my dad’s an accountant, and my mum’s a child play worker.  Erm but my er all my grandparents were engineers and their parents were engineers as well and my brother is as well.

Interviewer:	That’s quite interesting. When and why then do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Erm, well my granddad, he did aeronautical engineering, became an airline pilot, erm and or whatever aeronautical engineering was, back then.  Erm, and then I decided I wanted to be an airline pilot as well, but then after the terrorist attack on September 11th a lot of the airlines couldn’t afford to take on any pilots that didn’t have licences already. It costs a lot of money for them to fund a pilot to be trained – it’s about £100,000 or something, so erm, I had to – I couldn’t go straight from ‘A’ levels, to pilot training, so I decided to go to university and do something to do with aeroplanes, and then, hopefully, when I left I could like go back onto the original life plan that I had.

Interviewer:	What appealed to you about being an airline pilot?

Subject:	Erm, I dunno, just wanted to be one.  My granddad was one – I went to his retirement party, a and met a lot of other pilots, then I just thought yeah, this is the life for me.  It looked quite glamorous and it’s an opportunity to travel the world for free and get paid for it as well.  So, yeah.

Interviewer:	So have your family been supportive then of your choice then?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah ‘cos like I said my brother did engineering as well, so …

Interviewer:	He did aeronautical?

Subject:	No, he’s doing automotive.  Practically the same – so yeah, they kind of like us both and we support each other in it as well.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have much careers advice when you were at school?

Subject:	Er, yeah we – er my physics teacher was an aeronautical engineer so she’s the one that suggested doing it and pushed it, maybe a bit more.  Erm, but like I’d looked into pilot training, couldn’t fund it myself and you all had to be sponsored and when the opportunity for sponsorship wasn’t around any more I thought that maybe aeronautical engineering was a good idea, anyway.  Erm, but I didn’t – I wasn’t told of any university open days or anything like that. I found out about the one at [this university] from my physics teacher, but the careers like department, at school, they didn’t tell us about open days or careers fairs or anything that were at universities – we had to do that ourselves really.  But if you know where you want to go already it’s a bit easier I suppose.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and knowing what you want to do .OK, did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, well my dad’s side of it, was the civil engineer and he like commissions like buildings, hospitals and er schools and things and I – I thought about that. I thought about going into that but – and then I realised that it was – it just seemed a bit too – it wasn’t to do with – although it was to do with maths and physics, which I do like, it wasn’t going to help me potentially be a pilot afterwards.  I mean even if I didn’t become a pilot, after this course, I could still work with aeroplanes – something that I enjoy, erm, but with civil engineering or something I couldn’t do that and bridges and dams just don’t appeal to me at all.

Interviewer:	Did you ever look at the air transport management course here?

Subject:	Erm, I did, but you don’t do it, do you? (No) It feels too easy.  Only people who usually get like really ‘A’ level grades, I don’t think – I think they tell you to do aeronautical instead, because – I don’t know – I got erm 2 A’s and 2 B’s and like I’ve got friends that got like B’s, that did air transport management, so I thought I don’t want to – I want to keep challenging myself and get the best degree that I can, instead of doing something that I know will be easier but probably won’t get me as far as I want to get (yeah) but I did think about it.  Erm, but then I think what they can do with air transport management; I could probably do with aeronautical engineering as well but still have other choices.  So I decided to go with that.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Erm, I heard it was one of the best for aeronautical eng – well engineering in general, erm I went to – I only had 3 main choices really and that was [university 2], [university 3] and [this university].  Erm, I couldn’t make it to the interview at [university 2], so I got declined – my application did.  Erm, and I got accepted at the [university 3] and [this university] and went to both universities for interviews and er tours and things and these facilities here are a lot better.  I felt that the [university 3] seemed to be relying on a reputation rather than what they actually had, whereas you walk into the department here and there’s an aeroplane sitting in front of you.  They’ve got a lot more contacts with the industry, at [this university] as well. I don’t think – well they didn’t really say much – I know [university 3] are linked to [company], but [this university] seems to be – I looked it up on the Internet, they’re praised for their contacts in industry and things like that. So I just chose [this university] and it’s closer to home as well.

Interviewer:	OK when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I – but then when you do sort of ‘A’ level physics, you kind of get used to being in a male dominated – like it’s sort of their domain really, or they think of it as theirs anyway.  Erm, there was a lot more boys in our class than girls.  Physics was pretty much even.  Further maths was exactly – there was only 4 of us in the class, there was 2 girls and 2 boys, and French was all female. So I guess I wasn’t that prepared for it but I knew that engineering was like physics and maths based and I kind of expected it.  When I went for my interview as well, there was just guys everywhere and 1 girl so I kind of expected it.

Interviewer:	It doesn’t bother you at all then?

Subject:	Erm, no not really because I’ve got a lot of male friends back home and they – I don’t know, I’m just used to them, I don’t – like there’s some girls I suppose who every boy they see is a potential boyfriend and I just see them as individual friends, so I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged, or enabled to take engineering?

Subject:	Erm, only if they want to really. I think the ones that want to do it, and the ones that don’t do it, just don’t want to. It’s not like it’s not advertised enough.  I just think it’s – that’s the way it goes, like a lot of girls like to do languages and things like that and a lot of boys want to take cars to bits and put it together. I know it sounds sexist but I think it’s – I don’t think that’ll ever change unless girls do engineering and I think the ones that do want to, do do it.  I don’t think they choose something else because of fear of the boys or something.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women are given the information to know what engineering is, in the first place, to make a decision whether they want to do it or not?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know ‘cos like, at my school, like with one of my physics teachers being an engineer, and – well the other one was an engineer as well actually – erm and my further maths teacher’s daughter was doing engineering, so she kind of encouraged like me to do engineering as well.  Erm, I kind of – I don’t know if it’s like that for everyone but it was – I felt encouraged to do it.  They were like do you like this? Yes.  Do you like that?  Yes.  Well you’ll like engineering then and stuff.   And so I just did it.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Er, I think you’ve got to be logical, obviously, have common sense, you’ve got to be creative as well, although you’ve got to have the common sense though, you’ve also got to think what if?  What if?  Erm, and I think you’ve got to have patience cos things go wrong and then they go wrong again, and then they go wrong again and you kind of try and keep trying to succeed and not give up on stuff.  Erm, you’ve got to have a clear head sometimes to realise what some of the stuff you do – what kind of relevance that bears to your career, because sometimes you sit there and you think what the Hell is going on here?  When you’re doing this crazy maths and you think, what does this apply to?  And you’ve just got to ask, like what’s this in real life and then they’ll tell you. I think, yeah, you’ve got to have patience and patience with the boys as well, if you’re a girl.

Interviewer:	Would you describe any of those characteristics as more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. Erm, men do tend to like just see black and white, whereas women can see the grey in the middle I suppose, erm but then on the other hand, I don’t think a lot of the guys on my course have any foresight – they can’t like erm I don’t know what the word – they can’t see a potential mistake or something potentially going wrong, whereas I ‘m thinking hold on, if this doesn’t work we’re not gonna get our work in on time – that kind of thing.  So, I dunno, I think that the girls tend to be a lot more organised, like we have 6 course work hand ins between Tuesday and Wednesday this week. I’ve got all of mine in last week and the boys were working till 4 O’clock in the morning but I mean, I know every single girl on my course and I know that every single one of them had it in before the Bank Holiday weekend so we could enjoy the weekend, and all the boys were working at like 2 O’clock in the morning so erm I think the girls are a lot more organised.  But then again, I don’t know, they seem to – sometimes the guys seem to really, really understand like a mechanical procedure or something whereas I won’t really have any idea. I have to see it in real life instead of on paper.  Erm, but I dunno really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are the advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think advantages – maybe erm – there’s like – there seems to be sort of pressure on companies to not discriminate against people because of their age, or their sex or their race, so I think being a girl, I reckon nowadays if a company was faced with a girl and a guy with equal erm ability, they’d choose the girl.  So that could be an advantage that erm, with equal opportunities and things, and with less girls graduating with engineering degrees, I think we might find it – obviously if we – we have to like get a good degree, but I think we might find it easier to get where we want, than the guys.  Erm, it’s – I can’t really think of any dis – sometimes, the lads’ll make a joke, and they’ll like say you’re doing a boys course, or are you a lesbian?  That kind of thing.  I don’t think they actually mean it.  Erm, and also some of the boys on the course, they think that if you’re a girl you’re stupid, but that works to your advantage if you’re stuck on a piece of course work, because you just play up to it, and then they help you.  Whereas, they don’t help each other.

Interviewer:	OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be ?

Subject:	Erm, not really.  Erm, I thought it would be a bit more design; a bit more erm contact with aeroplanes and a bit more lab work but I mean with all the recent strikes and things I know that they are really under funded and they can’t afford to let us do a lot of practical work and run wind tunnels and things all the time but I think there’s a lot more theory than I expected. I thought there’d be a bit more practice but I can handle that. Some – a lot of people have left because they – they can’t do maths day in and day out, but they wanted to see like cars and planes and things but I’m OK with it, even though it wasn’t what I expected, it’s still not that different.

Interviewer:	How many people do you think have dropped out of your course?

Subject:	Off my course. I don’t know. I’d say out of I think there was 80 originally, or 70 – I’d say there’s about 55 now. I don’t know I’m trying to picture, to picture my lecture theatre – I mean 3 of my own friends have left and I mean, I’d say if I’m in a group of sort of 10 people and 3 of those have left, then out of 70, you’d think that like it would be in a proportion – I don’t know – there’s an engineer talking. I don’t know, I reckon about 10/15 people have left.  I don’t know.

Interviewer:	And how many girls are on your course?

Subject:	There were 6 to start off with and there’s 6 now – none of the girls dropped out.

Interviewer:	What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, the worst has to have been the January exam this year, where we had 6 exams in 8 days and 4 of them were in a row like Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday – that was the worst thing ever about the course because I just – people tried to put in a bad performance, and it wasn’t allowed and I felt that it was really demanding, especially cos they started like so soon after the Christmas holidays. Erm, and I suppose the best thing was like still passing them all and getting above average.  Apparently, the best is yet to come like a lot of 3rd years have told me that we’re gonna do a flight test course thing and that’s about the best thing on the course – like that’s the most fun. You spend a week like taking readings off an aeroplane and going up in the sky and stuff so, I’m expecting that to be the best.

Interviewer:	Are you glad that you took the course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, er 1 – she teaches us about [topic] – [name].  I think she’s our course admissions tutor as well (right OK) but yeah, she teaches us.  She’s nice.

Interviewer:	Do you think that – it’s probably difficult to tell if you’ve only had one female lecturer, but do you think that she’s got a different style of teaching to say the male teachers?

Subject:	No, not really.  She just – if anything she seems to expect more of us, but then maybe that’s because of her position in the department as well.  She’s got like people beneath her. She’s probably used to getting what she wants quite quickly, so I don’t know.  No, she was just like – just the same as the others.  Clearer – easier to understand, she did explain things differently but then every lecturer is like that.  So, I found her easier to understand but other people found other people.

Interviewer:	OK, would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, not really. I don’t – like I said, with it being male dominated you expect your lecturers to be male as well and I think – I’m not sure, but I think some of them are retired from the RAF and armed forces and things, so you just expect those to be male too. I know you shouldn’t, but you do.  Erm, I mean my personal tutor’s female. Erm, and we’ve got that female lecturer but it doesn’t make any difference whether it’s a girl or a woman or a man teaching us.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat the students all equally?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I think they do. One of my lecturer’s is always like – jokes around when I – well, there was this really loud bang in the workshop whilst we were cutting steel with a guillotine and you have to stamp on this board to get the blade to go through the steel and this piece of steel fell and it was visually – and I screamed.  He was like Oi, girl.  You’re the only girl in the workshop and I turned up with open toed sandals on and I got sent home because I had to wear shoes that covered my toes and you get little comments then but they don’t treat you differently for anything else.

Interviewer:	Does it bother you when you get comments like that then or …?

Subject:	No, because it was stupid to turn up to a workshop, where you’re gonna be handling equipment, wearing open toed sandals.  I didn’t think about it – it was summer.  Erm, I  mean yeah – if you scream, when you know it’s gonna make a noise, that was just ridiculously girly as well.  I expected it.

Interviewer:	As a woman in a male environment do you ever feel like you’re not expected to be girly and feminine, but that you’re expected to be like one of the lads.?

Subject:	Yeah, they don’t expect you to be girly at all.  Like the first time my course saw me out, wearing a skirt, they were like whoa, you’ve got legs!  You know, you’re not wearing a cap.  So, maybe I think – no, they don’t expect it at all really.  A lot – I think – it’s probably horrible but they do expect you to be gay as well.  They think that you’re really blokey – and I don’t know why they expect that, maybe it’s just a stereotype – they say the same about the girls’ rugby team and that kind of thing.  Erm, but they – they expect you to at least be able to get on with guys and to get on with guys you can’t be that girly really, I suppose.  Erm, to handle the course and handle all the men as well.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with the personal tutor that you’ve got – do you find them approachable?

Subject:	Erm, I’ve only ever spoken to her face to face twice and once was – they were both in my first year, one was after my summer you know – yeah, one was after my winter exam results and one was when I first started university but like I don’t – there was a death in my family recently, and I told my personal tutor and she told my lecturers and people that my course work was supposed to be handed to, that it wouldn’t all be in on time, that kind of thing.  And she was really good with that.  And, she’s also quite – she’ll talk to you on your own level because she’s got her children at university, or they’ve just graduated or something, so she knows the score, she doesn’t expect you to have 150% attendance for every single lecture – and 98% in all your course work and she doesn’t expect you to not go to the Union, so she’s quite cool, because she knows what it’s like.  If anything like – if someone tries to stop you from doing something, you want to do it even more I suppose. But erm my first set of exam results – first ever, weren’t that good because I was used to the ‘A’ level way of doing things and she just asked me about it and then, after my second set of results, last year, that were a lot better she er – she was like, oh nice to see you on your feet now and that was it really.  So…

Interviewer:	Does your first year count here?

Subject:	No, it didn’t but I think it was – if the first year’s anything, that the other years are supposed to go by then I think she was a bit worried, because I got sort of 40’s and early 50’s a lot and then, in the first semester, and she was like that’s just a pass, it’s not even like a 2:1.  Erm, then, in the second semester, I got sort of high 60’s and 70’s – then she was happy.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Since I started…?

Interviewer:	The course?

Subject:	The course.  Probably my 2 house mates because they do engineering as well.  You interviewed them both, they’re Samantha and Natalie (pseudonyms).  Erm, because they both get exactly the same as me.  A lot of guys on their course, a lot of male friends, erm, I don’t know – there’s no one really influences me, to be honest.  That sounds like I’m made of stone, but I make my own decisions.

Interviewer:	No that’s good.  OK, have you had to do much group work as part of your course?

Subject:	Not that much like Samantha and Natalie, they do civil and architectural engineering and they – it seems like they do it in groups all the time and I think I’ve erm 3 or 4 since I’ve been here – 3 or 4 pieces of group work and I absolutely hate it.  And they had some pieces of course work, where it was optional, you could do it on your own or do it in a group and share the marks, and I was like I’m doing it on my own.  I hate group work.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	Because boys are just useless and the chances of me being in a group, with other girls is very slim. I just think let me work on my own.  They’re not useless but the last group I was in, they – they actually said from the start, we’ll do an all nighter the night before it’s supposed to be handed in and I was like er no, I’m an 8 hours a night girl. I’m going to sleep.  So I did all my work, all my part of the course – the work – gave it to them, like over email and then they really resented the fact that that night they were doing an all nighter, I was out with my friends.  But that’s why I don’t like it, and it’s just too much running after people, trying to organise things.  And there’s one guy who’s always in my group because he’s like behind in the alphabet but he’s also in the RAF and he’s – he uses it as an excuse not to go to group meetings, every single time, so it just – it’s annoying, because being a girl as well, they kind of expect you to organise meetings and things.  Erm, if anything, like the way sometimes girls play up to the fact that they’re female, the guys will do exactly the same and they’ll say, come on, you do it. You’re a girl.  You know you’re better at this than us, so you end up in a position where you’re in charge of everyone and they just don’t do what you wan them to do.

Interviewer:	Have you worked with girls in groups as well?

Subject:	Erm, I can’t remember – yeah, I think I had a girl in my group erm the very first thing I did I think. I think I had a girl in my group when we went to the [name] Museum, but that was a one day piece of course work – we just had to walk around the plane and write down everything we could see and then write up stuff about it.  So we didn’t – I didn’t have to organise a meeting because it was compulsory anyway.  But apart from that no.

Interviewer:	Do you think that girls would be better to work with then?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know really because I know a girl on my course who I mix with, and she’s very up for organisers as well, so.  Erm, but then there’s like – then there’s – one of my best male friends, on the course, is really, really organised as well and me and him we’ll help each other with course work and things and be quite willing to start that kind of thing, weeks before the hand in, just to get it over and done with.  So, erm, I think females in general are more organised but then I suppose the kind of girls that end up on this course aren’t exactly the most girly girls or anything.  They’re not really that bothered either.  They, obviously, start acting like the people you’re friends with, after a while. I dunno.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any advantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, if you’re with someone really clever, and the marks are shared equally then you get some of their marks, I suppose.  Also, like erm some guy would be really good at putting – putting work together and presenting it nicely, and somebody else would be really good at public speaking, so you give them most of the presentation time and someone else would be really good at like maths and calculations, they could do that side of things.  So, the advantage of group work is wherever your shortcomings are, you’re guaranteed that somebody else is really good at what you’re not good at, so you get the best of everything in the end.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the experience of group work will help you when you get into the industry as well?

Subject:	Erm, well I’m not doing a placement and that’s because I don’t think I want to work in the industry when I’m finished.  So, I can’t really comment on that I suppose. If I did go into the industry I would probably still avoid group work.  

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s realistic?

Subject:	Erm, I actually don’t know what it’s like in industry, because I haven’t done a placement.  But then I think with the civil engineering people, they do so much group work because it’s all group work when they leave, and I think maybe that’s why we do less group work, because in real life, in the aerospace industry, there might be less group work – I don’t know.  Or maybe they know how much we hate it and how rubbish we are at it.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide not to go on placement then?

Subject:	Well yeah.  Well I started the course and I, at the end of the first year, I just – I started to think I like this for now, but I thought can I do this till I’m 65?  And I thought, I don’t think I can.  And because my teacher’s had engineering degrees, I thought maybe teaching was something to go into.  But, like I said before, one of the reasons I did the course was because it was to push to myself to the absolute limit, like it was – BEng degrees were higher than my final A level group.  So I got in, luckily, and I think – I just wanted to get the best degree and know that you can do anything really afterwards – with an aeronautical engineering degree.  Obviously you can’t be a lawyer or a doctor but you could go into business or finance or teaching or even the police force or something, so I think I just did it to give myself a lot of options and the possibility of working with aeroplanes as well.  But I don’t know.  I’ve got some work experience at [company] over the summer.  Because I’m not doing a placement anymore, I thought I’ll try and get experience anyway.  Erm, so I worked at [company], all of last summer and I’ve got some experience at [company] this summer and I’ll do something else next summer.  So I’ll see how it goes at [company] because if it’s good then I might think OK, it could be for me after all.

Interviewer:	What are you doing with them?

Subject:	Erm, they’re sending me to [place] to work at a – at the place where they design the wings.  Because the wings are designed and manufactured in England and they’re sent over to France with like with everything else that they’ll put together, so I’m gonna, I managed to make a friend of a friend and emailed him and said what I liked and that I liked designing things, but that I don’t like certain other things.  And he said well, you’ll be perfect if you went to [place] and have a look at wing design.  And also there, they’re just starting a new project which he said I could get involved with, so that should look good on my CV.

Interviewer:	You haven’t ruled out – next year – with an engineering company then?

Subject:	I think – I’ve obviously ruled out certain aspects of the course, but then there’s other things that I still really like.  So I’ll have a look at those in my final year projects and if it still goes good then I’ll do it.  But I couldn’t do what some people have done and get sponsored from the start, and sign a contract saying you’ll work for someone, when you haven’t got your degree yet.  I couldn’t do that because some of my friends have done it and they’ve – it’s like there’s no way out. It’s nice to have options.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there would have been any advantages in doing a placement?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, obviously you’d have friends within the industry – you’d have a foot in the door, whatever company you do your placement with.  But, er like after working at [company], they said they’ve have me back any time I want and this thing with [company] – I’m sure that a month there will be the same – like I’ll still make as much of an impression, as I could if I were there for longer. So I think it’s – I can still get myself to the same position where I’ve got opportunities in the industry when I leave.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the work experience that you’ve had already will help you when you do go and find a job, whether it’s in the industry or not?

Subject:	Erm, I think that – ‘cos I worked at [company] and the company have got a really good reputation, then the reputation of the company will – with that on my CV, the fact that I’ve worked for a company that’s known for like erm having been a highly successful company – I think that’ll help me.  But the experience itself, with it being within marketing, and I was working in customer relations – if that’d help me find summer jobs, like at [theme park] or something but it hasn’t – it won’t help me – I don’t think it’ll help me in – but some companies will obviously see it and go oh, you worked for [company], oh and [company].  So the names of companies will help but not what I actually do within.

Interviewer:	OK. If you did go into the industry then, do you know what type of company you’d like to work for?

Subject:	What do you mean?  Like er within the industry – what kind of part of the industry?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Oh somewhere where you don’t get your hands dirty. That’s the girl coming out of me.  

Interviewer:	That’s interesting because you said that you thought that the course would have more hands on stuff.

Subject:	Yeah, I thought it would have more hands on stuff like – not like, obviously engines and oil, that kind of thing – like designing and making erm – I don’t mind – I could do that with metal things, but I wouldn’t want to have to wear overalls to work every day.  Er, I think I dunno, because at physics ‘A’ level, you did a lot of experiments and things and it was fun writing them up and stuff to get an idea of what’s going on. I think that’s why it was important for me to do the same thing for the degree – to – just to understand what’s going on really, ‘cos when you see stuff on paper, and you see more and more on paper, and it’s all based on other stuff you’ve seen on paper, you start to lose track of what stuff actually is and you know all these names of things and components but you don’t actually know where they are in real life, and it starts to get a bit confusing.  But it would really help er my understanding while I’m here but then, when I leave, I don’t want to – I want to – I think design is more my kind of thing – er more maths and numbers than like cutting up sheets of metal and things.  But then essentially I have – you know, they say when you finish people do the cutting up of metal for you. You’re the one that – you do all the top level stuff and then they’re the one that finishes off and actually manufactures things.  You’ve got someone else doing it – labour that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	What sorts of things do you think will attract you to a company?  Will you look at things like location and money?  Or will the type of work that they do be more important do you think?

Subject:	I’d rather get paid less but be able to get out of bed and go to work everyday than get paid more and absolutely hate what I do like for 5 days a week.  So money – obviously I don’t want to get a degree here to earn the same as someone that has walked straight out of school erm but I – I also, I’m not obsessed with it.  And location doesn’t bother me at all.  Anywhere in the world really erm so long as they’re English or French speaking.  Erm, so that’s not anywhere in the world, is it?  No, like America, Australia, Canada – anywhere like that. That’d be fine cos I mean my family are dotted all over the world anyway, so I’d just be another addition for the holiday possibilities.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think would be the best and worst things about working in the engineering industry?

Subject:	Erm, erm well one of my dad’s friends once said – cos I told him what I was doing and he was like yeah, everyone’s an engineer and people tend to think that, like whether you’re an electrician or plumber or er or whether you design Concorde, that you’re just all in the same group of people that keep the world running really, I suppose. So I think maybe – but no I can’t think of anything bad to do with being – working in engineering. I mean there’s obviously – I think the industry’s quite short of engineers at the moment so like now, getting a job should be easier although getting a well paid job is another question.  But I don’t think there’s anything really particularly good or particularly bad about it. It’s like any degree really and any type of work.  I suppose the good thing is that you could do other stuff – you’re not tied to it forever.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

Subject:	In 5 years?  Er dunno.  Erm, in 5 years time I definitely want to have a job and a house – I don’t want to be living at home – and working – I would like to work in aerospace because with an aeronautical engineering degree, you’d get more money in aerospace because you’re qualified for what they want you for and because there’s not that many of us, they have to offer you more money to do it, I suppose.  Erm, I would – preferably, to make me feel like the degree was worthwhile, I would like to be working in aerospace, but it’s not completely 100% necessary. I have actually been looking into a PGCE to look at teacher training so I don’t really know.

Interviewer:	Ok, what about in say 10 years time?  Do you think you might go into management or anything like that?

Subject:	Yeah, like I said before like all the – all the hands on stuff and all that kind of thing, would be really good for the degree and I understand fully everything that’s going on, and get good exam grades and just leave with full knowledge of the subject but then, like I don’t want to – I think management would be good, sort of something – you feel like if you were gonna work 4 years for a masters and then maybe do extra, after that, like a PhD or something, you feel like you deserve to not actually erm you know, drive a white van or whatever.  You know the – you want to – you don’t want to have to settle for anything – when you’ve worked so hard you want to – you want to be – I don’t know what the word is – head hunted almost.  You think that you deserve that kind of appreciation for what you’ve done, but obviously there’s thousands and thousands of students that all want the same.  They all want everyone to think they’re the best thing in the world, so. Erm, but management would be good – something – I want to progress in whatever I do. If I became a teacher, I wouldn’t want to teach primary school kids for the rest of my life. I’d want to be Head of Department or Deputy Head of school, that kind of thing. I wouldn’t – you want to progress in whatever you do really.

Interviewer:	OK, would being an airline pilot feature in your ideal career?

Subject:	It is. I talk about it a lot but there’s also a part of me that’s resigned to the fact that I’d be absolutely rubbish at it.  I’ve flown 3 simulators and crashed all 3.  My hand/eye co-ordination is rubbish, I’d bump into things that have been in my room for the past 15 years and trip over and drop things, so I’d be really rubbish pilot but also it would be just great to be one.  But then pilots don’t really fly planes any more they just make sure the computer that does it for them doesn’t crash. That’s what they do really. It’s the computer that does it all now, so not that skilled. I don’t think hand/eye co-ordination, unless you’re gonna fly for the RAF and do aerobatics and things.  I think airline pilots, you don’t need to be that amazing any more.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s still a possibility that you might do that?

Subject:	Er, if – the only possible way I could do it – well there’s 2, you know like join the RAF and then when you retire – cos they retire quite young, then do it – you’re qualified to fly erm airlines – retired military pilots because they’re still young enough to work for another 20 years and they’re disciplined. The other way is fund it yourself and you’ll never ever be able to get that kind of money together, or get sponsored by the airline and [company] they’re – they can’t even pay their baggage handling staff at the moment, I don’t think. So right now, it’s still not a possibility.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in aeronautical engineering?

Subject:	Er, I suppose it’s – most of my friends have found placements without that much trouble, so I suppose there are quite a lot of opportunities still but I don’t know what it’s like for graduates. I had a look at summer placements within technology companies and things – the department secretary sent things round, but a lot of them wanted you to be in your penultimate year and I’m not.  So next year, that’ll be a possibility but I suppose because they can gauge how well you’re gonna do when you graduate whereas right now, I’m only half way through, so dunno.

Interviewer:	When did you start thinking that you might not want a career in engineering?

Subject:	Er, it was during the first year when er, the – I don’t know – obviously university’s not representative of the actual industry but erm it’s – I haven’t got enough passion for it, not as much as I thought I would have erm and like I said, then if I’m not gonna enjoy it then I’d rather get paid less to do something I do enjoy. (yeah) Or get paid more, in the case of an airline pilot.  So, erm, yeah, I don’t know – I can’t exactly pinpoint it.  I think, probably, even before I started the course I knew that I might not end up doing it for a living, but then my boyfriend’s got a history degree and works in PR and his friend’s got a law degree and works in PR as well.  So I – it – although I was scared at first I thought nah, I’ll just get the best degree I can and see where it takes me. (Yeah) But I have – I don’t really – there’s the dream of being a pilot that I could still do, but apart from that there’s literally quite a few things that I’ve thought about but literally nothing that I’m going to pursue yet.

Interviewer:	You don’t regret choosing this course at all then?

Subject:	No, if I was gonna do any course apart from this, it would be pure maths.  So, and that’d be just boring. I’m only good at maths and numbers really, so it was either engineering or maths.  I suppose I could have done French but I just – I don’t like – the good thing about engineering is, when you get work, you know whether you’ve done it right or wrong, and with a subject like French, or whatever, you write an essay and they check it for grammar and things – I don’t like that kind of things.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry or your experience of engineering?

Subject:	5 words? (Yeah) Er, erm, I think male has to be one of them – obviously – erm er, interesting, it’s quite exciting as well, I think in aerospace it’s more so because you’ve got the military side of things and they do some crazy stuff with planes, and that’s really cool.  What have I said?  Interesting, male, exciting, hard er no, change hard to challenging – challenging, interesting, exciting, male and er rewarding.  It’s definitely rewarding – when you get something done, when you’ve finished, or like in the case of last week when I had 6 pieces of work and I just threw them all into the reception like – yeah, you’ve done it – you feel brilliant at times.  So it’s cool.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think that it is male?  Is that literally to do with the numbers of men in the industry, or do you think it’s more than that?

Subject:	It’s for – it’s like what we said before – like the amount of men on the course, the amount of men in industry, the amount of men that are teachers, the amount of men that do it and the fact that when our lecturers teach us, they say he, he, he, whereas they say, now imagine a man and he’s doing this, and he’s doing that – it’s never – they never imagine a female in the scenario.  It’s just – you always consider it but it’s like people always think of teachers as being female, don’t they? (Yeah) They always think of – well, not so much – the doctors used to just be male and lawyers used to just be male, although there’s a lot more females getting into that now, and engineering has been slow to catch up with getting more women involved in it. But I don’t think it will ever catch up. I just think, women – if they don’t want to do it, they’re not gonna do it and there’s nothing you can do to get them to do it.

Interviewer:	If the situation has changed in things like medicine and law, though, do you think that it might change in engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I think no, because I think before like the situation is just – everything was male dominated because they just thought women could stay at home and cook.  And then when everything got a lot more equal, women had the opportunity to do anything they want, they chose to break into things like medicine and law and stuff and they chose not to go into engineering.  Every woman has got the opportunity to do it, and if they still don’t want to then it’s just – it must just be what it involves.  It puts people off.  If – they’ve got the opportunity and I think engineering is – is encouraged just as much as medicine and law and that kind of thing erm I don’t think it’s considered that professional. I think that might be what it is.  Like a doctor’s a considered professional and lawyers and stuff but eng – I don’t think engineering’s got that kind of clean cut professionalism linked to it, so women don’t think that they want to be involved with it.  I don’t know – I don’t know why.

Interviewer:	It’s not thought of so highly, is that what you mean?

Subject:	Yeah. I think – although you’re, although with an aeronautical engineering degree, you’re probably – you know, you can’t gauge how clever you are but someone who graduates from a 4 year law course and someone who graduates from a 4 year aero degree, you’re both obviously very good at what you do, but, for some reason, the lawyer seems to be a lot more – look a lot more professional than the person with the engineering degree.  So I don’t know – I think…

Interviewer:	Do you think that goes back to the perception of engineering being dirty and …?

Subject:	Yeah because people – I’ve got to admit I thought when I first started, I thought it would be as bad. I’ve said a lot more dirty, a lot more hands-on, like saws and drilling and rivets and things.  The bits that we have done like that are cool, and I guess, I don’t know – I think once you’re into it, then you know it’s not like that but before you get into it, you don’t think that. And that’s why before I got into it, I kind of already knew I wasn’t going to do it for the rest of my life, ‘cos I thought it could be cutting up metal for the rest of my life. I just did it ‘cos it had high entry grades and it said if you’re an engineer you’re very versatile and employable, so I thought that’s what I want to be – employable.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything, thank you very much, it’s all very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, we are interviewing women from all the different engineering disciplines – people in their 2nd year. We’re mainly interviewing people that are going on placement, because we want to know why they’re going on placement and what they expect to find out and we’re going back to them, when they’re on placement, again – but you’re not going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I was on the placement programme but then I changed to the actual one without the industrial placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well I’d be quite interested in why you made that decision then, that’s why we wanted to talk to you as well. The things that we’re looking at are why women decided to do engineering and hopefully try to improve women’s retention in the industry. At the end of the 2 year project, we’re going to put together a big guidance document (yes) and give it back to the Engineering Council to hopefully improve the situation for women (right) in engineering. So I’ll start off just asking you a few background questions about why you decided to do engineering and that. Is it aeronautical engineering that you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, aeronautical, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you doing the masters course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did French, Maths, Further Maths and Physics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Comprehensive – normal high school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It wasn’t an all girls’ school or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, just a regular.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Before I decided to do engineering at uni?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or while you’ve been at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no I wouldn’t say – I mean I worked at [company] but that’s more agricultural engineering and I worked in their marketing department, so didn’t have any hands-on experience or anything because it was business really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no, my dad’s an accountant, and my mum’s a child play worker. Erm but my er all my grandparents were engineers and their parents were engineers as well and my brother is as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite interesting. When and why then do you think that you decided to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well my granddad, he did aeronautical engineering, became an airline pilot, erm and or whatever aeronautical engineering was, back then. Erm, and then I decided I wanted to be an airline pilot as well, but then after the terrorist attack on September 11th a lot of the airlines couldn’t afford to take on any pilots that didn’t have licences already. It costs a lot of money for them to fund a pilot to be trained – it’s about £100,000 or something, so erm, I had to – I couldn’t go straight from ‘A’ levels, to pilot training, so I decided to go to university and do something to do with aeroplanes, and then, hopefully, when I left I could like go back onto the original life plan that I had.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What appealed to you about being an airline pilot?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I dunno, just wanted to be one. My granddad was one – I went to his retirement party, a and met a lot of other pilots, then I just thought yeah, this is the life for me. It looked quite glamorous and it’s an opportunity to travel the world for free and get paid for it as well. So, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So have your family been supportive then of your choice then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah ‘cos like I said my brother did engineering as well, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: He did aeronautical?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, he’s doing automotive. Practically the same – so yeah, they kind of like us both and we support each other in it as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have much careers advice when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah we – er my physics teacher was an aeronautical engineer so she’s the one that suggested doing it and pushed it, maybe a bit more. Erm, but like I’d looked into pilot training, couldn’t fund it myself and you all had to be sponsored and when the opportunity for sponsorship wasn’t around any more I thought that maybe aeronautical engineering was a good idea, anyway. Erm, but I didn’t – I wasn’t told of any university open days or anything like that. I found out about the one at [this university] from my physics teacher, but the careers like department, at school, they didn’t tell us about open days or careers fairs or anything that were at universities – we had to do that ourselves really. But if you know where you want to go already it’s a bit easier I suppose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and knowing what you want to do .OK, did you ever consider doing any of the other types of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well my dad’s side of it, was the civil engineer and he like commissions like buildings, hospitals and er schools and things and I – I thought about that. I thought about going into that but – and then I realised that it was – it just seemed a bit too – it wasn’t to do with – although it was to do with maths and physics, which I do like, it wasn’t going to help me potentially be a pilot afterwards. I mean even if I didn’t become a pilot, after this course, I could still work with aeroplanes – something that I enjoy, erm, but with civil engineering or something I couldn’t do that and bridges and dams just don’t appeal to me at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever look at the air transport management course here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I did, but you don’t do it, do you? (No) It feels too easy. Only people who usually get like really ‘A’ level grades, I don’t think – I think they tell you to do aeronautical instead, because – I don’t know – I got erm 2 A’s and 2 B’s and like I’ve got friends that got like B’s, that did air transport management, so I thought I don’t want to – I want to keep challenging myself and get the best degree that I can, instead of doing something that I know will be easier but probably won’t get me as far as I want to get (yeah) but I did think about it. Erm, but then I think what they can do with air transport management; I could probably do with aeronautical engineering as well but still have other choices. So I decided to go with that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I heard it was one of the best for aeronautical eng – well engineering in general, erm I went to – I only had 3 main choices really and that was [university 2], [university 3] and [this university]. Erm, I couldn’t make it to the interview at [university 2], so I got declined – my application did. Erm, and I got accepted at the [university 3] and [this university] and went to both universities for interviews and er tours and things and these facilities here are a lot better. I felt that the [university 3] seemed to be relying on a reputation rather than what they actually had, whereas you walk into the department here and there’s an aeroplane sitting in front of you. They’ve got a lot more contacts with the industry, at [this university] as well. I don’t think – well they didn’t really say much – I know [university 3] are linked to [company], but [this university] seems to be – I looked it up on the Internet, they’re praised for their contacts in industry and things like that. So I just chose [this university] and it’s closer to home as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK when you decided to do engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I – but then when you do sort of ‘A’ level physics, you kind of get used to being in a male dominated – like it’s sort of their domain really, or they think of it as theirs anyway. Erm, there was a lot more boys in our class than girls. Physics was pretty much even. Further maths was exactly – there was only 4 of us in the class, there was 2 girls and 2 boys, and French was all female. So I guess I wasn’t that prepared for it but I knew that engineering was like physics and maths based and I kind of expected it. When I went for my interview as well, there was just guys everywhere and 1 girl so I kind of expected it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It doesn’t bother you at all then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no not really because I’ve got a lot of male friends back home and they – I don’t know, I’m just used to them, I don’t – like there’s some girls I suppose who every boy they see is a potential boyfriend and I just see them as individual friends, so I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged, or enabled to take engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, only if they want to really. I think the ones that want to do it, and the ones that don’t do it, just don’t want to. It’s not like it’s not advertised enough. I just think it’s – that’s the way it goes, like a lot of girls like to do languages and things like that and a lot of boys want to take cars to bits and put it together. I know it sounds sexist but I think it’s – I don’t think that’ll ever change unless girls do engineering and I think the ones that do want to, do do it. I don’t think they choose something else because of fear of the boys or something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women are given the information to know what engineering is, in the first place, to make a decision whether they want to do it or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know ‘cos like, at my school, like with one of my physics teachers being an engineer, and – well the other one was an engineer as well actually – erm and my further maths teacher’s daughter was doing engineering, so she kind of encouraged like me to do engineering as well. Erm, I kind of – I don’t know if it’s like that for everyone but it was – I felt encouraged to do it. They were like do you like this? Yes. Do you like that? Yes. Well you’ll like engineering then and stuff. And so I just did it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics then, do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think you’ve got to be logical, obviously, have common sense, you’ve got to be creative as well, although you’ve got to have the common sense though, you’ve also got to think what if? What if? Erm, and I think you’ve got to have patience cos things go wrong and then they go wrong again, and then they go wrong again and you kind of try and keep trying to succeed and not give up on stuff. Erm, you’ve got to have a clear head sometimes to realise what some of the stuff you do – what kind of relevance that bears to your career, because sometimes you sit there and you think what the Hell is going on here? When you’re doing this crazy maths and you think, what does this apply to? And you’ve just got to ask, like what’s this in real life and then they’ll tell you. I think, yeah, you’ve got to have patience and patience with the boys as well, if you’re a girl.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe any of those characteristics as more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. Erm, men do tend to like just see black and white, whereas women can see the grey in the middle I suppose, erm but then on the other hand, I don’t think a lot of the guys on my course have any foresight – they can’t like erm I don’t know what the word – they can’t see a potential mistake or something potentially going wrong, whereas I ‘m thinking hold on, if this doesn’t work we’re not gonna get our work in on time – that kind of thing. So, I dunno, I think that the girls tend to be a lot more organised, like we have 6 course work hand ins between Tuesday and Wednesday this week. I’ve got all of mine in last week and the boys were working till 4 O’clock in the morning but I mean, I know every single girl on my course and I know that every single one of them had it in before the Bank Holiday weekend so we could enjoy the weekend, and all the boys were working at like 2 O’clock in the morning so erm I think the girls are a lot more organised. But then again, I don’t know, they seem to – sometimes the guys seem to really, really understand like a mechanical procedure or something whereas I won’t really have any idea. I have to see it in real life instead of on paper. Erm, but I dunno really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are the advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think advantages – maybe erm – there’s like – there seems to be sort of pressure on companies to not discriminate against people because of their age, or their sex or their race, so I think being a girl, I reckon nowadays if a company was faced with a girl and a guy with equal erm ability, they’d choose the girl. So that could be an advantage that erm, with equal opportunities and things, and with less girls graduating with engineering degrees, I think we might find it – obviously if we – we have to like get a good degree, but I think we might find it easier to get where we want, than the guys. Erm, it’s – I can’t really think of any dis – sometimes, the lads’ll make a joke, and they’ll like say you’re doing a boys course, or are you a lesbian? That kind of thing. I don’t think they actually mean it. Erm, and also some of the boys on the course, they think that if you’re a girl you’re stupid, but that works to your advantage if you’re stuck on a piece of course work, because you just play up to it, and then they help you. Whereas, they don’t help each other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. Erm, I thought it would be a bit more design; a bit more erm contact with aeroplanes and a bit more lab work but I mean with all the recent strikes and things I know that they are really under funded and they can’t afford to let us do a lot of practical work and run wind tunnels and things all the time but I think there’s a lot more theory than I expected. I thought there’d be a bit more practice but I can handle that. Some – a lot of people have left because they – they can’t do maths day in and day out, but they wanted to see like cars and planes and things but I’m OK with it, even though it wasn’t what I expected, it’s still not that different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many people do you think have dropped out of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Off my course. I don’t know. I’d say out of I think there was 80 originally, or 70 – I’d say there’s about 55 now. I don’t know I’m trying to picture, to picture my lecture theatre – I mean 3 of my own friends have left and I mean, I’d say if I’m in a group of sort of 10 people and 3 of those have left, then out of 70, you’d think that like it would be in a proportion – I don’t know – there’s an engineer talking. I don’t know, I reckon about 10/15 people have left. I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how many girls are on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There were 6 to start off with and there’s 6 now – none of the girls dropped out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the worst has to have been the January exam this year, where we had 6 exams in 8 days and 4 of them were in a row like Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday – that was the worst thing ever about the course because I just – people tried to put in a bad performance, and it wasn’t allowed and I felt that it was really demanding, especially cos they started like so soon after the Christmas holidays. Erm, and I suppose the best thing was like still passing them all and getting above average. Apparently, the best is yet to come like a lot of 3rd years have told me that we’re gonna do a flight test course thing and that’s about the best thing on the course – like that’s the most fun. You spend a week like taking readings off an aeroplane and going up in the sky and stuff so, I’m expecting that to be the best.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you glad that you took the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, er 1 – she teaches us about [topic] – [name]. I think she’s our course admissions tutor as well (right OK) but yeah, she teaches us. She’s nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that – it’s probably difficult to tell if you’ve only had one female lecturer, but do you think that she’s got a different style of teaching to say the male teachers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. She just – if anything she seems to expect more of us, but then maybe that’s because of her position in the department as well. She’s got like people beneath her. She’s probably used to getting what she wants quite quickly, so I don’t know. No, she was just like – just the same as the others. Clearer – easier to understand, she did explain things differently but then every lecturer is like that. So, I found her easier to understand but other people found other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. I don’t – like I said, with it being male dominated you expect your lecturers to be male as well and I think – I’m not sure, but I think some of them are retired from the RAF and armed forces and things, so you just expect those to be male too. I know you shouldn’t, but you do. Erm, I mean my personal tutor’s female. Erm, and we’ve got that female lecturer but it doesn’t make any difference whether it’s a girl or a woman or a man teaching us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the lecturers treat the students all equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I think they do. One of my lecturer’s is always like – jokes around when I – well, there was this really loud bang in the workshop whilst we were cutting steel with a guillotine and you have to stamp on this board to get the blade to go through the steel and this piece of steel fell and it was visually – and I screamed. He was like Oi, girl. You’re the only girl in the workshop and I turned up with open toed sandals on and I got sent home because I had to wear shoes that covered my toes and you get little comments then but they don’t treat you differently for anything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does it bother you when you get comments like that then or …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because it was stupid to turn up to a workshop, where you’re gonna be handling equipment, wearing open toed sandals. I didn’t think about it – it was summer. Erm, I mean yeah – if you scream, when you know it’s gonna make a noise, that was just ridiculously girly as well. I expected it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: As a woman in a male environment do you ever feel like you’re not expected to be girly and feminine, but that you’re expected to be like one of the lads.?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they don’t expect you to be girly at all. Like the first time my course saw me out, wearing a skirt, they were like whoa, you’ve got legs! You know, you’re not wearing a cap. So, maybe I think – no, they don’t expect it at all really. A lot – I think – it’s probably horrible but they do expect you to be gay as well. They think that you’re really blokey – and I don’t know why they expect that, maybe it’s just a stereotype – they say the same about the girls’ rugby team and that kind of thing. Erm, but they – they expect you to at least be able to get on with guys and to get on with guys you can’t be that girly really, I suppose. Erm, to handle the course and handle all the men as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with the personal tutor that you’ve got – do you find them approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’ve only ever spoken to her face to face twice and once was – they were both in my first year, one was after my summer you know – yeah, one was after my winter exam results and one was when I first started university but like I don’t – there was a death in my family recently, and I told my personal tutor and she told my lecturers and people that my course work was supposed to be handed to, that it wouldn’t all be in on time, that kind of thing. And she was really good with that. And, she’s also quite – she’ll talk to you on your own level because she’s got her children at university, or they’ve just graduated or something, so she knows the score, she doesn’t expect you to have 150% attendance for every single lecture – and 98% in all your course work and she doesn’t expect you to not go to the Union, so she’s quite cool, because she knows what it’s like. If anything like – if someone tries to stop you from doing something, you want to do it even more I suppose. But erm my first set of exam results – first ever, weren’t that good because I was used to the ‘A’ level way of doing things and she just asked me about it and then, after my second set of results, last year, that were a lot better she er – she was like, oh nice to see you on your feet now and that was it really. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does your first year count here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it didn’t but I think it was – if the first year’s anything, that the other years are supposed to go by then I think she was a bit worried, because I got sort of 40’s and early 50’s a lot and then, in the first semester, and she was like that’s just a pass, it’s not even like a 2:1. Erm, then, in the second semester, I got sort of high 60’s and 70’s – then she was happy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone or anything that you’d say has been like the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Since I started…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The course. Probably my 2 house mates because they do engineering as well. You interviewed them both, they’re Samantha and Natalie (pseudonyms). Erm, because they both get exactly the same as me. A lot of guys on their course, a lot of male friends, erm, I don’t know – there’s no one really influences me, to be honest. That sounds like I’m made of stone, but I make my own decisions.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No that’s good. OK, have you had to do much group work as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not that much like Samantha and Natalie, they do civil and architectural engineering and they – it seems like they do it in groups all the time and I think I’ve erm 3 or 4 since I’ve been here – 3 or 4 pieces of group work and I absolutely hate it. And they had some pieces of course work, where it was optional, you could do it on your own or do it in a group and share the marks, and I was like I’m doing it on my own. I hate group work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because boys are just useless and the chances of me being in a group, with other girls is very slim. I just think let me work on my own. They’re not useless but the last group I was in, they – they actually said from the start, we’ll do an all nighter the night before it’s supposed to be handed in and I was like er no, I’m an 8 hours a night girl. I’m going to sleep. So I did all my work, all my part of the course – the work – gave it to them, like over email and then they really resented the fact that that night they were doing an all nighter, I was out with my friends. But that’s why I don’t like it, and it’s just too much running after people, trying to organise things. And there’s one guy who’s always in my group because he’s like behind in the alphabet but he’s also in the RAF and he’s – he uses it as an excuse not to go to group meetings, every single time, so it just – it’s annoying, because being a girl as well, they kind of expect you to organise meetings and things. Erm, if anything, like the way sometimes girls play up to the fact that they’re female, the guys will do exactly the same and they’ll say, come on, you do it. You’re a girl. You know you’re better at this than us, so you end up in a position where you’re in charge of everyone and they just don’t do what you wan them to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you worked with girls in groups as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I can’t remember – yeah, I think I had a girl in my group erm the very first thing I did I think. I think I had a girl in my group when we went to the [name] Museum, but that was a one day piece of course work – we just had to walk around the plane and write down everything we could see and then write up stuff about it. So we didn’t – I didn’t have to organise a meeting because it was compulsory anyway. But apart from that no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that girls would be better to work with then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know really because I know a girl on my course who I mix with, and she’s very up for organisers as well, so. Erm, but then there’s like – then there’s – one of my best male friends, on the course, is really, really organised as well and me and him we’ll help each other with course work and things and be quite willing to start that kind of thing, weeks before the hand in, just to get it over and done with. So, erm, I think females in general are more organised but then I suppose the kind of girls that end up on this course aren’t exactly the most girly girls or anything. They’re not really that bothered either. They, obviously, start acting like the people you’re friends with, after a while. I dunno.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any advantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, if you’re with someone really clever, and the marks are shared equally then you get some of their marks, I suppose. Also, like erm some guy would be really good at putting – putting work together and presenting it nicely, and somebody else would be really good at public speaking, so you give them most of the presentation time and someone else would be really good at like maths and calculations, they could do that side of things. So, the advantage of group work is wherever your shortcomings are, you’re guaranteed that somebody else is really good at what you’re not good at, so you get the best of everything in the end.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the experience of group work will help you when you get into the industry as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I’m not doing a placement and that’s because I don’t think I want to work in the industry when I’m finished. So, I can’t really comment on that I suppose. If I did go into the industry I would probably still avoid group work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s realistic?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I actually don’t know what it’s like in industry, because I haven’t done a placement. But then I think with the civil engineering people, they do so much group work because it’s all group work when they leave, and I think maybe that’s why we do less group work, because in real life, in the aerospace industry, there might be less group work – I don’t know. Or maybe they know how much we hate it and how rubbish we are at it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide not to go on placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well yeah. Well I started the course and I, at the end of the first year, I just – I started to think I like this for now, but I thought can I do this till I’m 65? And I thought, I don’t think I can. And because my teacher’s had engineering degrees, I thought maybe teaching was something to go into. But, like I said before, one of the reasons I did the course was because it was to push to myself to the absolute limit, like it was – BEng degrees were higher than my final A level group. So I got in, luckily, and I think – I just wanted to get the best degree and know that you can do anything really afterwards – with an aeronautical engineering degree. Obviously you can’t be a lawyer or a doctor but you could go into business or finance or teaching or even the police force or something, so I think I just did it to give myself a lot of options and the possibility of working with aeroplanes as well. But I don’t know. I’ve got some work experience at [company] over the summer. Because I’m not doing a placement anymore, I thought I’ll try and get experience anyway. Erm, so I worked at [company], all of last summer and I’ve got some experience at [company] this summer and I’ll do something else next summer. So I’ll see how it goes at [company] because if it’s good then I might think OK, it could be for me after all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What are you doing with them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, they’re sending me to [place] to work at a – at the place where they design the wings. Because the wings are designed and manufactured in England and they’re sent over to France with like with everything else that they’ll put together, so I’m gonna, I managed to make a friend of a friend and emailed him and said what I liked and that I liked designing things, but that I don’t like certain other things. And he said well, you’ll be perfect if you went to [place] and have a look at wing design. And also there, they’re just starting a new project which he said I could get involved with, so that should look good on my CV.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You haven’t ruled out – next year – with an engineering company then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I’ve obviously ruled out certain aspects of the course, but then there’s other things that I still really like. So I’ll have a look at those in my final year projects and if it still goes good then I’ll do it. But I couldn’t do what some people have done and get sponsored from the start, and sign a contract saying you’ll work for someone, when you haven’t got your degree yet. I couldn’t do that because some of my friends have done it and they’ve – it’s like there’s no way out. It’s nice to have options.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there would have been any advantages in doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, obviously you’d have friends within the industry – you’d have a foot in the door, whatever company you do your placement with. But, er like after working at [company], they said they’ve have me back any time I want and this thing with [company] – I’m sure that a month there will be the same – like I’ll still make as much of an impression, as I could if I were there for longer. So I think it’s – I can still get myself to the same position where I’ve got opportunities in the industry when I leave.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the work experience that you’ve had already will help you when you do go and find a job, whether it’s in the industry or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think that – ‘cos I worked at [company] and the company have got a really good reputation, then the reputation of the company will – with that on my CV, the fact that I’ve worked for a company that’s known for like erm having been a highly successful company – I think that’ll help me. But the experience itself, with it being within marketing, and I was working in customer relations – if that’d help me find summer jobs, like at [theme park] or something but it hasn’t – it won’t help me – I don’t think it’ll help me in – but some companies will obviously see it and go oh, you worked for [company], oh and [company]. So the names of companies will help but not what I actually do within.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. If you did go into the industry then, do you know what type of company you’d like to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What do you mean? Like er within the industry – what kind of part of the industry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh somewhere where you don’t get your hands dirty. That’s the girl coming out of me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s interesting because you said that you thought that the course would have more hands on stuff.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I thought it would have more hands on stuff like – not like, obviously engines and oil, that kind of thing – like designing and making erm – I don’t mind – I could do that with metal things, but I wouldn’t want to have to wear overalls to work every day. Er, I think I dunno, because at physics ‘A’ level, you did a lot of experiments and things and it was fun writing them up and stuff to get an idea of what’s going on. I think that’s why it was important for me to do the same thing for the degree – to – just to understand what’s going on really, ‘cos when you see stuff on paper, and you see more and more on paper, and it’s all based on other stuff you’ve seen on paper, you start to lose track of what stuff actually is and you know all these names of things and components but you don’t actually know where they are in real life, and it starts to get a bit confusing. But it would really help er my understanding while I’m here but then, when I leave, I don’t want to – I want to – I think design is more my kind of thing – er more maths and numbers than like cutting up sheets of metal and things. But then essentially I have – you know, they say when you finish people do the cutting up of metal for you.
