You’re the one that – you do all the top level stuff and then they’re the one that finishes off and actually manufactures things. You’ve got someone else doing it – labour that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sorts of things do you think will attract you to a company? Will you look at things like location and money? Or will the type of work that they do be more important do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d rather get paid less but be able to get out of bed and go to work everyday than get paid more and absolutely hate what I do like for 5 days a week. So money – obviously I don’t want to get a degree here to earn the same as someone that has walked straight out of school erm but I – I also, I’m not obsessed with it. And location doesn’t bother me at all. Anywhere in the world really erm so long as they’re English or French speaking. Erm, so that’s not anywhere in the world, is it? No, like America, Australia, Canada – anywhere like that. That’d be fine cos I mean my family are dotted all over the world anyway, so I’d just be another addition for the holiday possibilities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think would be the best and worst things about working in the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, erm well one of my dad’s friends once said – cos I told him what I was doing and he was like yeah, everyone’s an engineer and people tend to think that, like whether you’re an electrician or plumber or er or whether you design Concorde, that you’re just all in the same group of people that keep the world running really, I suppose. So I think maybe – but no I can’t think of anything bad to do with being – working in engineering. I mean there’s obviously – I think the industry’s quite short of engineers at the moment so like now, getting a job should be easier although getting a well paid job is another question. But I don’t think there’s anything really particularly good or particularly bad about it. It’s like any degree really and any type of work. I suppose the good thing is that you could do other stuff – you’re not tied to it forever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In 5 years? Er dunno. Erm, in 5 years time I definitely want to have a job and a house – I don’t want to be living at home – and working – I would like to work in aerospace because with an aeronautical engineering degree, you’d get more money in aerospace because you’re qualified for what they want you for and because there’s not that many of us, they have to offer you more money to do it, I suppose. Erm, I would – preferably, to make me feel like the degree was worthwhile, I would like to be working in aerospace, but it’s not completely 100% necessary. I have actually been looking into a PGCE to look at teacher training so I don’t really know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what about in say 10 years time? Do you think you might go into management or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, like I said before like all the – all the hands on stuff and all that kind of thing, would be really good for the degree and I understand fully everything that’s going on, and get good exam grades and just leave with full knowledge of the subject but then, like I don’t want to – I think management would be good, sort of something – you feel like if you were gonna work 4 years for a masters and then maybe do extra, after that, like a PhD or something, you feel like you deserve to not actually erm you know, drive a white van or whatever. You know the – you want to – you don’t want to have to settle for anything – when you’ve worked so hard you want to – you want to be – I don’t know what the word is – head hunted almost. You think that you deserve that kind of appreciation for what you’ve done, but obviously there’s thousands and thousands of students that all want the same. They all want everyone to think they’re the best thing in the world, so. Erm, but management would be good – something – I want to progress in whatever I do. If I became a teacher, I wouldn’t want to teach primary school kids for the rest of my life. I’d want to be Head of Department or Deputy Head of school, that kind of thing. I wouldn’t – you want to progress in whatever you do really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would being an airline pilot feature in your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is. I talk about it a lot but there’s also a part of me that’s resigned to the fact that I’d be absolutely rubbish at it. I’ve flown 3 simulators and crashed all 3. My hand/eye co-ordination is rubbish, I’d bump into things that have been in my room for the past 15 years and trip over and drop things, so I’d be really rubbish pilot but also it would be just great to be one. But then pilots don’t really fly planes any more they just make sure the computer that does it for them doesn’t crash. That’s what they do really. It’s the computer that does it all now, so not that skilled. I don’t think hand/eye co-ordination, unless you’re gonna fly for the RAF and do aerobatics and things. I think airline pilots, you don’t need to be that amazing any more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s still a possibility that you might do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, if – the only possible way I could do it – well there’s 2, you know like join the RAF and then when you retire – cos they retire quite young, then do it – you’re qualified to fly erm airlines – retired military pilots because they’re still young enough to work for another 20 years and they’re disciplined. The other way is fund it yourself and you’ll never ever be able to get that kind of money together, or get sponsored by the airline and [company] they’re – they can’t even pay their baggage handling staff at the moment, I don’t think. So right now, it’s still not a possibility.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in aeronautical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I suppose it’s – most of my friends have found placements without that much trouble, so I suppose there are quite a lot of opportunities still but I don’t know what it’s like for graduates. I had a look at summer placements within technology companies and things – the department secretary sent things round, but a lot of them wanted you to be in your penultimate year and I’m not. So next year, that’ll be a possibility but I suppose because they can gauge how well you’re gonna do when you graduate whereas right now, I’m only half way through, so dunno.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When did you start thinking that you might not want a career in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it was during the first year when er, the – I don’t know – obviously university’s not representative of the actual industry but erm it’s – I haven’t got enough passion for it, not as much as I thought I would have erm and like I said, then if I’m not gonna enjoy it then I’d rather get paid less to do something I do enjoy. (yeah) Or get paid more, in the case of an airline pilot. So, erm, yeah, I don’t know – I can’t exactly pinpoint it. I think, probably, even before I started the course I knew that I might not end up doing it for a living, but then my boyfriend’s got a history degree and works in PR and his friend’s got a law degree and works in PR as well. So I – it – although I was scared at first I thought nah, I’ll just get the best degree I can and see where it takes me. (Yeah) But I have – I don’t really – there’s the dream of being a pilot that I could still do, but apart from that there’s literally quite a few things that I’ve thought about but literally nothing that I’m going to pursue yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You don’t regret choosing this course at all then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, if I was gonna do any course apart from this, it would be pure maths. So, and that’d be just boring. I’m only good at maths and numbers really, so it was either engineering or maths. I suppose I could have done French but I just – I don’t like – the good thing about engineering is, when you get work, you know whether you’ve done it right or wrong, and with a subject like French, or whatever, you write an essay and they check it for grammar and things – I don’t like that kind of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry or your experience of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 5 words? (Yeah) Er, erm, I think male has to be one of them – obviously – erm er, interesting, it’s quite exciting as well, I think in aerospace it’s more so because you’ve got the military side of things and they do some crazy stuff with planes, and that’s really cool. What have I said? Interesting, male, exciting, hard er no, change hard to challenging – challenging, interesting, exciting, male and er rewarding. It’s definitely rewarding – when you get something done, when you’ve finished, or like in the case of last week when I had 6 pieces of work and I just threw them all into the reception like – yeah, you’ve done it – you feel brilliant at times. So it’s cool.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why do you think that it is male? Is that literally to do with the numbers of men in the industry, or do you think it’s more than that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s for – it’s like what we said before – like the amount of men on the course, the amount of men in industry, the amount of men that are teachers, the amount of men that do it and the fact that when our lecturers teach us, they say he, he, he, whereas they say, now imagine a man and he’s doing this, and he’s doing that – it’s never – they never imagine a female in the scenario. It’s just – you always consider it but it’s like people always think of teachers as being female, don’t they? (Yeah) They always think of – well, not so much – the doctors used to just be male and lawyers used to just be male, although there’s a lot more females getting into that now, and engineering has been slow to catch up with getting more women involved in it. But I don’t think it will ever catch up. I just think, women – if they don’t want to do it, they’re not gonna do it and there’s nothing you can do to get them to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If the situation has changed in things like medicine and law, though, do you think that it might change in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think no, because I think before like the situation is just – everything was male dominated because they just thought women could stay at home and cook. And then when everything got a lot more equal, women had the opportunity to do anything they want, they chose to break into things like medicine and law and stuff and they chose not to go into engineering. Every woman has got the opportunity to do it, and if they still don’t want to then it’s just – it must just be what it involves. It puts people off. If – they’ve got the opportunity and I think engineering is – is encouraged just as much as medicine and law and that kind of thing erm I don’t think it’s considered that professional. I think that might be what it is. Like a doctor’s a considered professional and lawyers and stuff but eng – I don’t think engineering’s got that kind of clean cut professionalism linked to it, so women don’t think that they want to be involved with it. I don’t know – I don’t know why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s not thought of so highly, is that what you mean?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think – although you’re, although with an aeronautical engineering degree, you’re probably – you know, you can’t gauge how clever you are but someone who graduates from a 4 year law course and someone who graduates from a 4 year aero degree, you’re both obviously very good at what you do, but, for some reason, the lawyer seems to be a lot more – look a lot more professional than the person with the engineering degree. So I don’t know – I think…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that goes back to the perception of engineering being dirty and …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah because people – I’ve got to admit I thought when I first started, I thought it would be as bad. I’ve said a lot more dirty, a lot more hands-on, like saws and drilling and rivets and things. The bits that we have done like that are cool, and I guess, I don’t know – I think once you’re into it, then you know it’s not like that but before you get into it, you don’t think that. I just did it ‘cos it had high entry grades and it said if you’re an engineer you’re very versatile and employable, so I thought that’s what I want to be – employable.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
